```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
options(digits = 3)
```

Models that predict how cells respond to a perturbation ("virtual cell"
models, in-silico knockouts) are usually compared with a handful of
metrics averaged over held-out perturbations. Those averages can mislead:

* when most perturbations shift expression in the same direction, a
  prediction that ignores the perturbation altogether can score well;
* when most perturbations barely change expression, every method scores
  alike because the measured change is mostly noise;
* raw scores have no fixed scale, so "0.54 versus 0.52" says nothing about
  how much of the achievable improvement a model has captured.

`pertEvalR` addresses these points in one workflow:

1. **diagnose** the dataset (`pe_signal()`);
2. **split** perturbations into training and held-out sets (`pe_split()`);
3. **predict** with reference baselines or your own model
   (`baseline_*()`, `pe_prediction()`);
4. **score** each held-out perturbation (`pe_evaluate()`);
5. **compare** methods with paired statistics (`pe_compare()`);
6. **calibrate** scores between an uninformative baseline and a technical
   replicate (`pe_bounds()`, `pe_calibrate()`);
7. **stratify** by how well each perturbation is measured (`pe_subset()`).

This vignette walks through the workflow on simulated data, so every step
runs in a few seconds.

```{r setup}
library(pertEvalR)
```

## 1. Data

A `pe_data` object holds a genes x cells matrix of log-normalized
expression and one perturbation label per cell. Control cells carry the
label given by `control`; combinations of perturbations are written with a
separator, by default `"+"` (for example `"KLF1+MAP2K6"`).

```{r data}
x <- pe_simulate(n_genes = 300, n_single = 60, n_combo = 30,
                 shared_effect = 0.3, noise_sd = 1, effect_spread = 1,
                 seed = 1)
x
```

`pe_simulate()` returns data with known effects: each single perturbation
knocks down its own target gene and changes a random set of other genes,
every perturbation adds a common shift whose size is set by `shared_effect`,
and `effect_spread` makes some perturbations much stronger than others, as in
real screens.

Your own data come in through `pe_data()` (any matrix or sparse matrix) or
directly from Bioconductor and Seurat objects:

```{r convert, eval = FALSE}
x <- pe_data(expr, perturbation = labels, control = "non-targeting")
x <- as_pe_data(sce, perturbation_col = "target_gene",
                control = "non-targeting")            # uses assay "logcounts"
x <- as_pe_data(seurat_obj, perturbation_col = "target_gene",
                control = "non-targeting")            # uses layer "data"
```

## 2. Diagnose the dataset first

Before comparing any models, `pe_signal()` describes what the data can
show. For each perturbation it reports the cosine similarity between its
change from control and the average change over all perturbations
(systematic variation), the effect size, the effective number of changed
genes, and the split-half reliability of the change.

```{r signal}
sig <- pe_signal(x, seed = 1)
sig
head(sig$per_perturbation)
```

The two summary numbers to look at first:

* **systematic fraction**: the share of all change that lies along the one
  average shift. When it is large, metrics that correlate predicted and
  observed change from control reward predicting that shift for every
  perturbation.
* **median reliability**: how reproducible the changes are between two
  random halves of the cells. When it is low, most perturbations have no
  measurable effect and no model can be told apart from a baseline on them.

A simulation with a strong common shift looks very different: almost all
of the change is the same for every perturbation.

```{r signal-compare}
pe_signal(pe_simulate(n_genes = 300, n_single = 60, n_combo = 30,
                      shared_effect = 2, seed = 1), seed = 1)
```

## 3. Split

`pe_split()` holds out perturbations, not cells. Two tasks are supported:

* `"unseen_single"`: predict single perturbations never seen in training.
  Combinations involving a held-out gene are removed from training, so its
  effect cannot leak in.
* `"unseen_combo"`: predict combinations whose single perturbations were
  all seen in training.

```{r split}
s <- pe_split(x, type = "unseen_single", test_frac = 0.25, seed = 42)
s
```

## 4. Predict

Four reference baselines cover the predictions any useful model has to beat:

| Baseline | Prediction for every held-out perturbation |
|---|---|
| `baseline_control()` | no change: the control profile |
| `baseline_mean()` | the average of the training perturbations |
| `baseline_additive()` | for combinations: control plus the sum of the single effects |
| `baseline_linear()` | the linear model of Ahlmann-Eltze et al. (2025) |

```{r baselines}
preds <- list(
  baseline_control(x, s),
  baseline_mean(x, s),
  baseline_linear(x, s, targets = x$sim$targets)
)
```

`targets` maps perturbation labels to target genes; when labels already are
gene names (as in most Perturb-seq screens), it can be omitted.

Predictions from your own model enter through `pe_prediction()`: a genes x
held-out perturbations matrix on the same scale as the data, with columns
named after `s$test`. Here, for illustration only, a "model" that peeks at
the held-out data and adds noise:

```{r own-model}
truth <- pe_truth(x, s)
set.seed(7)
my_pred <- truth + matrix(rnorm(length(truth), sd = 0.15), nrow(truth))
preds$my_model <- pe_prediction(my_pred, s, method = "my_model")
preds$my_model
```

## 5. Score

`pe_evaluate()` scores every method on every held-out perturbation and
returns one row per method, perturbation and metric.

```{r evaluate}
res <- pe_evaluate(preds, x)
head(res)
pe_summary(res)
```

| Metric | Measures | Better |
|---|---|---|
| `mse`, `mse_top` | squared error, over all genes / the `top_n` most changed genes | lower |
| `pearson_delta`, `pearson_delta_top` | correlation of predicted and observed change from control | higher |
| `pearson_delta_pert` | the same, but change from the average perturbed profile | higher |
| `pds` | how well the prediction identifies its own perturbation among all held-out ones (0.5 = chance) | higher |

Some metrics are undefined for some baselines (for example the correlation
with the change from control for the no-change baseline, which predicts no
change); those values are `NA`.

## 6. Compare

Means over a few dozen perturbations differ by chance. `pe_compare()` pairs
methods perturbation by perturbation and reports the mean difference, a
bootstrap confidence interval, a Wilcoxon signed-rank test with
multiple-testing correction, and which method the evidence favours,
respecting the direction of each metric.

```{r compare}
cmp <- pe_compare(res, reference = "mean", seed = 1)
cmp[cmp$metric %in% c("pearson_delta", "pds") & cmp$method_a != "control",
    c("metric", "method_a", "method_b", "n", "diff", "ci_low", "ci_high",
      "p_adj", "favours")]
```

## 7. Calibrate

A raw score means little until it is placed between two references:

* **lower bound**: the better of the no-change and training-mean baselines
  for that metric (score 0);
* **upper bound**: a technical replicate, obtained by predicting one random
  half of each held-out perturbation's cells from the other half and
  correcting to the full sample size (score 1).

```{r calibrate}
b <- pe_bounds(x, s, seed = 1)
cal <- pe_calibrate(res, b)
cal[cal$metric %in% c("pearson_delta", "pds"),
    c("method", "metric", "score", "lower", "upper", "calibrated")]
```

A calibrated score near 0 means "no better than ignoring the perturbation";
near 1 means "as good as measuring the perturbation again". Scores slightly
above 1 are possible because the replicate bound is estimated.

## 8. Stratify by measurement reliability

On real screens many perturbations have little measurable effect, and an
average over all of them mainly measures how methods fit noise.
`pe_subset()` restricts results and bounds to a chosen set of perturbations
while keeping the settings `pe_calibrate()` checks. Passing the
`pe_signal()` object selects perturbations by reliability; the threshold is
a property of the data and is fixed before any model is compared.

Reliability should track how strong a perturbation really is. The
simulation records each single perturbation's strength, so this can be
checked directly:

```{r reliability-check}
rel <- sig$per_perturbation
singles <- names(x$sim$strength)
cor(x$sim$strength, rel$reliability[match(singles, rel$perturbation)],
    method = "spearman")
```

Here the threshold is the median reliability of the held-out perturbations;
on real data a fixed value such as 0.5 is easier to report.

```{r subset}
threshold <- stats::median(rel$reliability[rel$perturbation %in% s$test])
res_rel <- pe_subset(res, sig, min_reliability = threshold)
b_rel <- pe_subset(b, sig, min_reliability = threshold)
cal_rel <- pe_calibrate(res_rel, b_rel)
cal_rel[cal_rel$metric == "pearson_delta",
        c("method", "n", "score", "lower", "upper", "calibrated")]
```

One caution: `pds` ranks each prediction against the other held-out
perturbations. An uninformative prediction is furthest from the
perturbations with the largest effects, so within a subset chosen by effect
size or reliability its `pds` is no longer 0.5. Interpret `pds` on subsets
through `pe_calibrate()`, whose lower bound is computed on the same
perturbations.

## 9. Combinations

The same steps apply to unseen combinations, where the additive baseline is
the natural reference:

```{r combos}
s2 <- pe_split(x, type = "unseen_combo", test_frac = 0.25, seed = 42)
res2 <- pe_evaluate(list(baseline_mean(x, s2), baseline_additive(x, s2)), x)
pe_calibrate(res2, pe_bounds(x, s2, seed = 1))[
  , c("method", "metric", "score", "calibrated")]
```

The additive baseline adds each component's change from control, and each of
those changes contains the common shift, so a pair receives the shift twice.
When systematic variation is strong this costs the additive baseline on
`mse`, while its correlation-based scores and `pds` stay high. This is one
more reason to read several metrics, each against its calibrated bounds.

## 10. A reporting checklist

When reporting a perturbation model evaluated with `pertEvalR`:

1. report `pe_signal()` for each dataset (systematic fraction, median
   reliability);
2. include the no-change and training-mean baselines, and the linear or
   additive baseline for the task;
3. report calibrated scores next to raw scores;
4. report paired differences with confidence intervals rather than means
   alone, pooled over several random splits;
5. when most perturbations are unreliable, report results for reliable
   perturbations separately.
